name: Basil
description: A fragrant, warm-season herb that is a staple in many cuisines, especially Italian. Very sensitive to frost.
tips: Harvest often by pinching stems just above a pair of leaves. This encourages the plant to become bushier and more productive.
succession: Sow seeds every 2-3 weeks for a continuous supply of young, tender leaves throughout the summer.
yield: Continuous harvest of leaves. A few plants can provide a steady supply for a family.

soil.notes: Does not require heavy fertilization. A light feeding of compost mid-season is sufficient.

temperature.notes: Very sensitive to frost and cool temperatures. Prefers warm days and nights (above 60°F).

environmentalAlerts.message: Cover with a blanket or bring potted plants indoors to protect from frost.

storage.notes: Keep fresh stems in a glass of water on the counter like a bouquet. Do not refrigerate, as leaves will turn black. Can be pureed with olive oil and frozen in ice cube trays.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Pinch back tips to encourage branching
careTasks.description: Once the plant has a few sets of leaves, pinch the top set off. This encourages the plant to grow bushy and full, maximizing your harvest.

careTasks.name: Remove flower buds
careTasks.description: Pinch off flower heads as soon as they appear. If the plant flowers, its leaf production slows and the flavor can change.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Basil thrives in evenly moist soil. Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Watering at the base of the plant helps prevent fungal diseases.

name: Cilantro
description: A fast-growing, cool-season herb. The leaves are called cilantro, and its seeds are known as coriander.
tips: Tends to bolt (go to flower) very quickly in heat. Provide afternoon shade in warmer climates to prolong the leaf harvest.
succession: Essential for a continuous supply. Sow new seeds every 2 weeks from spring until early fall, as plants bolt quickly.
yield: Continuous harvest of leaves for 4-6 weeks per planting, then coriander seeds.

soil.notes: Does not need overly rich soil, which can sometimes accelerate bolting.

temperature.notes: A cool-season herb. Bolts rapidly in temperatures above 85°F. Can tolerate a light frost.

environmentalAlerts.message: Cilantro can tolerate a light frost, but cover if a hard freeze is expected to extend the harvest.

storage.method: Refrigerate or freeze leaves; dry store seeds
storage.notes: Store leaf stems in a jar of water in the fridge, loosely covered. Leaves can also be chopped and frozen. Dry coriander seeds completely and store in an airtight container.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Thin seedlings to stand 4-6 inches apart to give them room to grow without overcrowding.

careTasks.name: Begin harvesting leaves
careTasks.description: Harvest outer leaves regularly, which can help delay bolting. Never remove more than one-third of the plant at a time.

careTasks.name: Harvest coriander seeds (optional)
careTasks.description: Once the plant bolts and flowers, allow the seeds to form and dry on the plant. Harvest when they turn brown, and store for culinary use.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Cilantro grows best in soil that is kept consistently moist, which helps prolong leafy growth and delay bolting. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry.

name: Parsley
description: A biennial herb typically grown as an annual, available in curly-leaf and flat-leaf (Italian) varieties.
tips: Soak seeds overnight before planting to speed up the notoriously slow germination. Parsley is a host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly caterpillar.
succession: Not typically needed as plants are productive all season long. Plant once in spring for a season-long harvest.
yield: Continuous harvest of leaves. A few plants are usually sufficient for family use.

soil.notes: Benefits from soil amended with plenty of compost. Consistent moisture is key for tender growth.

temperature.notes: Very cold-hardy and can often be harvested after a light frost, and sometimes into the winter in mild climates.

environmentalAlerts.message: Parsley is cold-hardy, but cover if a hard freeze is expected to extend the harvest.

storage.notes: Place stems in a glass of water in the refrigerator, or wrap the bunch in a damp paper towel and place in a plastic bag. Freezes well when chopped.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep the soil consistently moist, like a damp sponge, to help seeds germinate. Avoid letting the soil dry out completely.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Harvest outer stems
careTasks.description: Harvest the larger, outer stems first by cutting them at the base. This encourages the plant to produce new growth from the center.

careTasks.name: Monitor for swallowtail caterpillars
careTasks.description: Check for green, black, and yellow striped caterpillars. If you enjoy butterflies, consider planting extra parsley to share.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Parsley produces lush leaves with consistent moisture. Water deeply whenever the top inch of soil feels dry to the touch.
